company.hook: The fastest way to get more comments on your posts.
company.photocard_text: End with a specific, easy-to-answer question, not a generic "thoughts?". Specific questions get specific replies.
company.caption: Ending a post with "thoughts?" rarely gets a response, because it's too open-ended for most people to bother answering. Swapping that for a specific, low-effort question - one with an easy, obvious answer like picking between two options or naming a favorite from a short list - tends to get noticeably more replies, because there's almost nothing to think about before typing one. More comments also tends to help the post get shown to more people in the first place, so this small wording change can have a bigger effect than it looks like it should. Try it on your next post and see what happens to your comment count. We're happy to help you brainstorm a few if you'd like.

company.hook: How to pick a cover photo that actually works for you.
company.photocard_text: Your cover photo should answer "what do you do" in two seconds, not just look nice. Clarity beats decoration every time.
company.caption: A cover photo is one of the first things a new visitor sees, and a purely decorative one - a nice scene with no information - wastes that first impression. The cover photos that work hardest answer "what does this business do" at a glance: a clear shot of the product, the storefront, or the service in action, sometimes with a short line of text if the image alone doesn't make it obvious. It doesn't need to be elaborate, just immediately clear. If someone unfamiliar with your business landed on your Page right now, would your cover photo tell them what you do within two seconds? If not, it's worth a quick update. We can help you put one together.

company.hook: A client once wanted to delete every negative comment.
company.photocard_text: Hiding fair criticism doesn't protect a brand, it removes the chance to respond well in public and build more trust.
company.caption: A client once asked us to delete every comment that wasn't glowing, worried criticism on the Page would scare customers away. We pushed back. A fair complaint, answered calmly in public, usually builds more trust than a Page with suspiciously only positive comments - people assume a business with zero visible complaints is hiding something. We helped the client respond to the criticism instead of deleting it, and the public reply reassured far more people than the complaint worried anyone. Hiding fair feedback removes a chance to show how a business handles problems. Reach out if your Page needs help with this.

company.hook: We once posted the same offer three different ways.
company.photocard_text: Same discount, three different framings. One clearly outperformed the others, and it wasn't the one anyone expected.
company.caption: For one client we tested the same discount with three different framings in one week: one led with urgency, one with the savings amount, one with the problem it solved. The problem-led version, which nobody on the team expected to win, clearly outperformed the other two in engagement and messages received. It was a reminder that assumptions about what "should" work are worth testing rather than trusting on instinct. We run small tests like this regularly so decisions are based on what the audience actually responds to. Want help testing your next promotion a few ways? Message us.

company.hook: We learned not to post on a day we almost skipped.
company.photocard_text: A short, low-effort post on a quiet day once outperformed a week of planned content, just by showing up consistently.
company.caption: One week the planned content wasn't ready in time, and the easy choice would have been to skip posting that day entirely. Instead a short, simple post went up - a quick behind-the-scenes photo with a couple of honest lines - and it got more engagement than most of the carefully planned posts that same week. Planning still matters most of the time, but showing up consistently, even imperfectly, matters more than waiting for a perfect post. We now keep a few simple, low-effort post ideas in reserve for exactly these moments. Ask us how we build that backup plan into your schedule.

company.hook: Your Page's bio is doing less work than you think.
company.photocard_text: A vague bio makes a new visitor guess what you do. A clear one tells them in one line and points them to act.
company.caption: The Page bio is one of the most overlooked parts of a Facebook presence, even though it's often the first thing a new visitor reads before deciding to follow or scroll past. A vague bio - just a name and a generic tagline - leaves a visitor guessing what the business does and why they should care. A clear one states plainly what it offers and who it's for, in one or two lines, and points toward the next step. It takes minutes to rewrite but affects every new visitor who lands on the Page. Haven't revisited yours in a while? We're happy to help you sharpen it.

personal.hook: The simplest fix for a page that feels inconsistent.
personal.photocard_text: Write down your 3 non-negotiables before your next post: tone, colors, and the one thing you never say. Check every post against them.
personal.caption: A lot of "our page doesn't feel like us" problems aren't creative problems, they're documentation problems - nobody ever wrote down what "us" actually means in concrete terms. The fastest fix I use with clients is a one-page brand check: three or four non-negotiables, written in plain language, that every single post has to pass before it goes out. That might be a tone rule ("friendly, never salesy"), a visual rule ("always use our two brand colors, never stock photo people"), and a content rule ("we never post without a clear takeaway for the reader"). It sounds almost too simple to matter, but having it written down turns a vague feeling of inconsistency into a two-minute checklist anyone on the team can run before hitting publish, including a social media manager who joined last month and never sat through the original branding conversation. If your page feels off but you can't say exactly why, that's usually the sign the rules only exist in someone's head instead of on paper.

personal.hook: A client once asked me to post more. I said no.
personal.photocard_text: More posts isn't always the right answer. Sometimes the honest advice is to slow down and fix the message first.
personal.caption: Early on I would have said yes to almost anything a client asked for, because saying no felt like risking the relationship. One client wanted to double posting frequency to "fix" flat engagement. I looked at the numbers first and the problem wasn't frequency, it was that the posts weren't saying anything a follower actually cared about - doubling a weak message just means twice as much of it gets ignored. I said so directly, laid out what I was seeing, and proposed we fix the message before touching the schedule. It was an uncomfortable conversation to start, but it was the right one, and it's a pattern I now watch for constantly: when a client asks for more volume, the real question is always whether the existing content earns more attention first. Agencies that just say yes to every request aren't being helpful, they're avoiding a harder conversation. The lesson I keep relearning is that giving honest, sometimes unwelcome advice early is what actually earns trust, not agreeing with everything a client suggests.

personal.hook: I used to chase every new platform. I stopped.
personal.photocard_text: Being everywhere with a weak presence loses to being consistently good on two platforms that actually fit your audience.
personal.caption: There was a stretch where I felt pressure to have a presence on every platform the moment it started trending, because it felt irresponsible not to, like I was leaving growth on the table. What actually happened was predictable: thin, inconsistent content spread across too many places, none of it good enough to build real momentum anywhere. The turning point was picking two platforms where the actual audience for a given business already spends time, committing to doing those two well, and deliberately ignoring the rest for now. Engagement and inquiries both improved once the effort stopped being spread so thin. The lesson wasn't "never try new platforms," it was that presence without depth doesn't build trust with anyone, it just produces more surface area to look inconsistent on. Now, before adding any new platform for a client, I ask whether we can genuinely sustain a second strong channel, not whether the platform is popular. Depth beats breadth almost every time in social media.

personal.hook: The post I almost didn't publish got the best response.
personal.photocard_text: The polished, safe post I was proud of got ignored. The honest, slightly messy one about a real mistake got shared.
personal.caption: I had a post ready that was polished, on-brand, and said exactly nothing risky - the kind of post that's easy to approve and easy to scroll past. At the last minute I swapped it for something rougher: a short, honest note about a mistake made early in managing a client's page and what changed afterward. I almost didn't post it because it felt less "professional" than the planned content. It ended up getting far more genuine engagement than almost anything else that month, because it read like a person talking instead of a brand performing. The lesson stuck with me: audiences can tell the difference between content that's trying to look impressive and content that's actually trying to be useful or honest, and they respond to the second kind even when it's less polished. I still plan posts carefully, but I leave room now for the slightly riskier, more human version of an idea instead of always defaulting to the safest draft.

personal.hook: Stop writing captions before you know who they're for.
personal.photocard_text: One paragraph on your actual audience - their worry, their habit, their platform - will sharpen every caption you write after it.
personal.caption: Caption writing gets dramatically easier the moment you stop trying to write for "everyone who might see this" and start writing for one specific kind of person. I ask every client to write a short, plain paragraph describing that one person: what they're worried about, what platform habit they already have, what would make them trust a business like this one. It's not a formal persona document, just a page's worth of honesty about who actually buys from them. Once that exists, caption writing stops being a guessing game, because every line can be checked against a real question: would this specific person care about this sentence. Posts written this way tend to read more direct and less generic, because they're not trying to please a vague audience of nobody in particular. If your captions feel bland even though you're working hard on them, the issue usually isn't your writing skill, it's that you're writing toward an audience you haven't actually defined yet.
